FlatSAM2 · design record · generated by experiments/build_tracker_cards.py

Tracker Cards

The tracker between WOFTSAM/SAM-H and today. WOFT, WOFTSAM and SAM-H are assumed known; everything else is defined here. Each mechanism is given as equations plus the function that implements it, each figure is that function running on real frames, and each claim carries the measurement that supports it — including the ones that came out against the design.

0.2 Symbols

  • C = [c₁ c₂ c₃ c₄], the 2×4 control points: image positions of the template's four corners in fixed cyclic order. θ = vec(C) ∈ ℝ⁸ is what every solver here optimizes.
  • H(C): the homography taking the template corners to C (the 4-point parameterization). No solver touches raw 3×3 coefficients — that choice is what makes §3.3 work.
  • M_t: the SAM3 mask of frame t. D_t: its signed distance field, negative inside, in pixels. B = {b₁ … b_N}: N points sampled on the template silhouette's contour (N = 150).

0.3 Metric and aggregation

et= 14 ∑k=14 ∥c^k −ckGT∥2 P@τ= 100|V| |{t∈V: et≤τ}|

V = all valid annotated frames of all sequences, first frame excluded. This pooled form — every frame counts once — is the aggregation the benchmark success plots use and equals overall_p@k in evaluate.py. PTi pools 133,320 frames over 300 sequences; POT-210 pools 1,004 over 210 (its GT is sparse).

Warning. docs/state-of-the-tracker.md and older journal entries quote per-sequence means instead, which weight a 14-frame sequence like a 2 500-frame one. Numbers here differ from those documents; on MPOT-3K the two even disagree in sign. The pooled number is the one to quote.

br-P@15 is P@15 after choosing, per frame, the cyclic relabeling of the predicted corners that minimizes the error; gap = br-P@15 − P@15 separates corner naming from localization.

1 · Two branches, one question

Both branches consume the same SAM3 mask stream and output four corners with a 2×2 covariance each. The keypoint branch (LMr) matches texture and fits a homography by MAGSAC on the correspondences inside the mask dilated by 10 px. The mask branch estimates the pose from the silhouette alone. Everything in §3–§6 is about the mask branch's estimator and how the two are combined.

ORACLE is not a tracker: it picks, per frame, whichever branch is closer to the ground truth. Its PTi P@15 of 91.24 against SWITCH35's 87.68 bounds what any combination rule can buy.

2 · What the mask branch optimizes

Implementation: flatsam2/mask_align.py::_gn_align. One objective, stated once.

ri(θ)= Dt( H(C)⋅bi ), i=1…N E(θ)= ∑i ρδ(ri (θ)), ρδ(r)= { r22 |r|≤δ δ(|r|− δ/2) |r|>δ

In words: warp the template outline by the candidate pose, and measure how far each of its sampled points lands from the current mask's boundary, where D_t = 0. δ = 5.0 px. Only the outline enters, so the objective is defined for any shape and is blind to texture — which is exactly the weakness §5 has to repair.

2.1 The solver

(J⊤WJ +λI) Δθ=− J⊤Wr, Wii= { 1|ri| ≤δ δ/|ri| |ri|>δ

J = ∂r/∂θ by forward differences (0.5 px step), λ Levenberg damping starting at 1, halved on an accepted step and quadrupled on a rejected one; stop at max|Δθ| < 0.05 px or 60 iterations. W is the IRLS weight of the Huber loss, so a sample beyond δ is down-weighted, not discarded.

3 · Corner covariance — derivation and validation

Both branches must speak the same language for §6 to be possible. This is the whole construction, and then the check that it is true.

3.1 The recipe, step by step

Both branches run the same seven steps; they differ only in step 1 and step 2. Nothing below is specific to masks or to keypoints, which is the whole point — it is what lets the two report uncertainty in one currency.

  1. Fix what is being estimated. θ = (x₁,y₁,x₂,y₂,x₃,y₃,x₄,y₄) ∈ ℝ⁸ — the four corner positions in the current frame, and nothing else. Any θ determines a homography H(θ): the unique projective map taking the four template corners to those four points (cv2.getPerspectiveTransform, an 8×8 solve). Why this parameterization and not the 8 entries of H: the answer we want is the corners, so their covariance will fall out with no change of variables. Parameterize by H and you must afterwards push the covariance through the warp Jacobian — an extra approximation for nothing.
  2. Take the evidence, and write one residual per piece of it. A residual answers: if the corners were θ, how wrong would this one piece of evidence be?
    • Mask branch — take the N = 156 template boundary points b_i, sampled evenly along the outline of the template silhouette, and the signed distance field D_t of this frame's SAM3 mask (§2). Warp each b_i by H(θ) and read the field there: r_i(θ) = D_t(H(θ)·b_i), one number per point. Zero means that boundary sample landed exactly on the mask's edge, which is what a correct pose does.
    • Keypoint branch — take the MAGSAC inlier correspondences 𝓘 = {(p_i, q_i)}: p_i a template-frame keypoint, q_i its match in this frame. Warp p_i and compare: r_i(θ) = H(θ)·p_i − q_i, two numbers per correspondence, so the stacked vector is 2|𝓘| long. Zero means that match is reprojected exactly onto its partner.
    Both stack into one vector r(θ) with as many rows as there are pieces of evidence. Both are already the objective the branch minimized — this is not a new model fitted afterwards.
  3. Differentiate the residuals with respect to the corners. For each of the 8 coordinates in turn: move that one coordinate by ±0.5 px, recompute the entire residual vector both times, and take the central difference. That fills one column of J, so J is (rows = evidence) × 8 and costs 16 residual evaluations. Why by finite differences rather than analytically: r goes through getPerspectiveTransform and a bilinear field lookup; ±0.5 px is well inside the smooth regime, matches the aligner's own step, and smaller steps lose to cancellation rather than gaining accuracy. J is where all the geometry lives: entry (i, p) says how strongly evidence i responds to moving corner coordinate p. Evidence that does not respond does not constrain that corner — which is exactly what a large uncertainty ellipse is reporting.
  4. Weight the rows the way the fit did. W is diagonal: 1 for the keypoint branch, the fit's own Huber weights w_i = min(1, δ/|r_i|) for the mask branch. The covariance must describe the estimator that actually ran; a row the solve down-weighted did not get a full vote in θ̂ and must not get one here.
  5. Get the noise scale from the fit's own residuals. σ̂² = Σ w_i r_i² / (N − 8). N − 8, not N, because eight parameters were fitted to this same data — the residuals are that much smaller than the true noise. There is no external noise model anywhere: the fit's own misfit is the estimate of how noisy its evidence was.
  6. Invert the normal matrix. This is the standard first-order covariance of a weighted nonlinear least-squares estimate at its converged point:
Σθ= σ^2 (J⊤WJ) −1, σ^2= ∑iwi ri2 N−8

Why an inverse, when J points the wrong way

Step 3 measures how wrong the evidence goes when a corner moves — ∂r/∂θ. What we want is the opposite: how far a corner moves when the evidence moves — ∂θ/∂y. The two are connected, and the inversion in the formula above is that connection, not a bookkeeping detail.

θ̂ is not an explicit function of the evidence — it is whatever minimizes the fit, defined implicitly. So it cannot be differentiated directly. Instead differentiate the condition that defines it. At the optimum the gradient vanishes, and r = f(θ) − y, so ∂r/∂y = −I:

J⊤Wr( θ^,y) =0 ⇒ J⊤WJ δθ − J⊤W δy =0 ∂θ^ ∂y = (J⊤WJ) −1 J⊤W

Solving for δθ gives the sensitivity we actually wanted, ∂θ̂/∂y = (JᵀWJ)⁻¹JᵀW. Propagating evidence noise through it, Cov(θ̂) = (∂θ̂/∂y) Cov(y) (∂θ̂/∂y)ᵀ, collapses to σ̂²(JᵀWJ)⁻¹ whenever Cov(y) = σ²W⁻¹. The forward Jacobian is the only differentiable object on the path, which is why it is computed "backwards" and then inverted.

The scalar case makes it obvious. With one parameter and rᵢ = c·θ − yᵢ, where c is how strongly that corner drives the residual: JᵀJ = Nc², so Σ = σ²/(Nc²) — and directly, δθ = δy/c. ∂θ/∂y is one over ∂r/∂θ. A corner whose movement barely disturbs the residuals is a corner that evidence noise can shove a long way before the fit objects; a corner whose movement wrecks the fit immediately is pinned. J is the stiffness of the fit against moving each corner; the covariance is the compliance, stiffness inverted and scaled by how noisy the evidence is.

Which is also why the two readings are the same statement: "the evidence goes badly wrong when this corner moves" is precisely what it means for that evidence to be informative about the corner. JᵀWJ is the Fisher information; covariance is inverse information. Sensitivity, information and 1/variance are one quantity read three ways.

What "the evidence moves" is, concretely. For the mask branch y is where SAM3's boundary actually sits, so the covariance answers: had SAM3 drawn this silhouette slightly differently, where would this corner have landed? For the keypoint branch y is the matched point positions, and the same question is asked of match jitter.

Caveat this derivation exposes. The collapse to σ̂²(JᵀWJ)⁻¹ needs Cov(y) = σ²W⁻¹, i.e. weights that are inverse variances. The mask branch's W holds Huber weights, chosen for robustness against a boundary that is partly wrong, not because they are inverse variances. Strictly the sandwich (∂θ̂/∂y) Cov(y) (∂θ̂/∂y)ᵀ therefore does not collapse and we use the convenient form anyway. That is a second, independent source of miscalibration alongside the correlated residuals of §3.3, and part of why the deployed scale corrections (§6.2) are as large as they are.

  1. Read the corners off the diagonal. Because θ is the corner positions, Σ_k is simply the 2×2 diagonal block of Σ_θ for corner k — no propagation step. The off-diagonal blocks, i.e. how corner 1's error correlates with corner 3's, are computed and then discarded; §6 treats the four corners as independent. That is a real approximation and the honest place to flag it: the corners of one fitted quad are correlated, so the fusion is not using the full joint covariance it could. Finally each Σ_k's eigenvalues are clamped from below at (0.25 px)². A near-singular normal matrix — a boundary arc too short to pin an axis — otherwise produces an eigenvalue near zero, i.e. a claim of near-certainty, and any Mahalanobis distance computed against it explodes; values near 10⁸ were observed in the field.

Implementations, line for line the same formula: flatsam2/mask_align.py::_corner_cov_from_boundary_fit and flatsam2/corner_covariance.py::homography_corner_covs.

3.2 What J looks like on a real frame

Since every claim about which corner is uncertain is a claim about J, here is J itself, computed by the deployed code on real data — each boundary sample coloured by ‖∂r_i/∂c_k‖, its sensitivity to moving corner k one pixel.

What the covariance means, and what it does not. It is how far this corner would move if the evidence this branch used were resampled — a sampling-noise model. It cannot know the evidence is the wrong object: a confident fit to a distractor gives a tight, wrong ellipse. Gross-error rejection is a separate mechanism (§6's gate), not something the covariance can provide.

3.3 Validation on real data, and where it breaks

The direct check is to resample the evidence and see where the corners actually land. Two resamplings: an i.i.d. bootstrap over the boundary samples (the assumption the closed form makes) and a moving-block bootstrap with block length L = 5 (which preserves runs of correlated residuals).

closed form σ (px)i.i.d. bootstrap σ block bootstrap σblock / closed form
corner 00.860.451.041.21
corner 11.101.754.063.68
corner 20.622.505.739.22
corner 30.570.601.232.16

The reason is physical: the samples are ordered along the contour, and a mask boundary error is spatially smooth, so neighbouring residuals err together. The measured autocorrelation of r along the contour gives the effective sample size the independence assumption over-counts:

Neff= Nτint, τint=1+2 ∑k>0 ρk, ρk=corr( ri,ri+k)

Measured on this frame: τ_int = 5.1 samples, so N_eff = 31 of 156 boundary points. That predicts a σ inflation of √τ_int = 2.25×; the block bootstrap measures 2.92× (median over corners), against 1.32× for the i.i.d. bootstrap. So most of the closed form's optimism is explained from first principles by correlated residuals, and the correction is computable per frame at no cost — τ_int comes from the residual vector the solver already has.

4 · Propose → refine → verify

A single solve from the last pose only works when the last pose is nearly right, which is when the branch is not needed. So the pose is searched. Implementation: flatsam2/mask_register.py::register_mask.

4.1 Propose

Whitening a silhouette by the inverse square root of its second-moment matrix leaves it defined up to a rotation, so two whitened silhouettes agree up to exactly one angle:

A(φ)= Wmask−1 R(φ) Wtpl, W•= Σ• −1/2

Sweeping φ over 24 steps enumerates every affine pose the two shapes' second moments are consistent with — no corners, lines or convexity anywhere, so it is defined for any shape. Reflections are excluded: a planar object seen from the front cannot mirror. The last-frame pose and any externally supplied pose enter as proposals alongside the sweep.

4.2 Refine

The 4 best proposals get a coarse GN solve (long side 256 px), the best 2 of those a full-resolution solve. The solve is §2, unchanged.

5 · The verification score, from first principles

This is the part that most deserved the accusation of being convoluted. Here is what it is, what justifies it, and what the data says about its parameters.

5.1 What is being asked

Given a candidate pose, two independent pieces of evidence are available: the warped template silhouette should coincide with the mask, and the surface under the warped template should look like the template. Writing the two agreements as likelihood terms and taking their log gives a log-linear pool — a weighted sum of log-evidence, i.e. a weighted geometric mean of the two agreements:

logs= alogIoU +blog 1+NCC2

with IoU the raster intersection-over-union of the warped silhouette against M_t, and NCC the normalized cross-correlation of the warped template's grey values against the frame, computed only inside warp ∧ M_t so occluders and background never enter the sum. (1 + NCC)/2 maps correlation to [0, 1]. The deployed setting is a = 2.0, b = 0.5; ranking uses s, so any monotone rescaling is irrelevant and only the ratio a : b matters.

Two things follow immediately and are worth stating plainly: the exponents are weights on two log-evidence terms, not tuning knobs with independent meaning; and a third factor that used to sit in this product — a sharpness term in the fit residual — is disabled (residual_power = 0) because the residual was measured to separate right from wrong poses only weakly.

5.2 Do the weights matter? (offline benchmark, PTi test, 961 cases per regime)

gooddriftlostcoldp90 lostp90 cold
a=2, b=0.5 (deployed)86.684.179.379.4151173
a=2, b=186.584.380.580.3117129
a=1, b=186.583.680.079.9115114

P@15 by initialization regime; the last two columns are the 90th-percentile corner error in pixels. Within a : b from 2 : 0.5 to 1 : 1 the metric moves by at most 0.7 pp anywhere, so the weights are not identifiable from this data and should not be presented as tuned parameters. The simple choice a = 2, b = 1 is as good or better everywhere except 0.1 pp in good, and cuts the p90 error substantially when the pose is lost. What is not optional is the second term at all: dropping it (b = 0) costs 13 pp — see §7's ablation.

5.3 A defect this figure exposed, and its fix

In that panel the returned pose (left, 342 px from GT, score 0.770) is beaten by its own +1 relabeling (20.9 px, score 0.859). Cause: alias_shortcut compares relabelings of coarsely refined proposals, and the full-resolution solve then moves the pose with nothing re-examining its naming.

The obvious fix — re-score the winner's three relabelings — loses 3.0 pp P@15 in the good regime while gaining 0.9 when lost, because a naming inherited from the previous frame carries temporal evidence the single-frame score does not, and a noisy score then flips correct namings. Requiring an inherited naming to be beaten by the same margin a challenger pose must clear restores that:

gooddriftlostcoldp90 lostp90 cold
no re-check (deployed)86.684.179.379.4151173
alias re-check86.684.480.179.8129143

Corrected rule: good unchanged at 86.6, lost 79.3 → 80.1, and the p90 error when lost 151.4 → 128.7 px. Shipped as register_alias_recheck (config corner_fusion_register_recheck). FINAL+RECHECK on the full grids: PTi 87.62 P@15 (-0.14 against FINAL), POT 97.61.

6 · Fusing the branches — and whether per-corner is justified

Implementation: flatsam2/tracking/corner_fusion.py::fuse_corners.

6.1 The rule

dk2= (ak− bk)⊤ (Σa,k +Σb,k )−1 (ak−bk) c^k= (Σa,k−1 +Σb,k−1) −1 (Σa,k−1 ak+ Σb,k−1 bk)

a_k, b_k are the two branches' corner k, with covariances Σ_a,k and Σ_b,k. When the two agree the corner is the precision-weighted average above; when they disagree the rule takes the branch with the smaller covariance trace. A missing branch is zero precision, so it drops out with no special case. G = 20.

The decision is taken once for the whole quad, not four times. The original rule compared d²_k ≤ G per corner, so its output could take two corners from one branch and two from the other — a pose neither branch ever proposed. §6.3 measures what that freedom is worth (almost nothing) and §6.5 measures what removing it is worth (a real gain). The shipped rule (fusion.decision_scope='whole_frame') tests the mean of the four d²_k against the same G — under the same model the sum over four corners is χ²₈, so the mean keeps G in its original χ²₂ units — and then either fuses every corner or hands the whole pose to the more confident branch.

6.2 Calibration — this is not probabilistic fusion

Under a correct Gaussian model d²_k is χ²₂ (median 1.39, 95% at 5.99). Deployed: covariances are multiplied by 32 (keypoint) and 70 (mask) before the gate, and G = 20 sits above the χ² quantile on top of that. §3.3 explains part of it from first principles — correlated residuals cost a factor ≈8.5 in variance — but not a factor of 70. The remainder is model error: bias in the mask, and fits to the wrong object, which no resampling covariance can see. Honest description: a relative precision model with an empirical scale correction, and a tuned gate. The per-frame τ_int correction of §3.3 is the obvious way to replace part of the fudge with something derived; it is not yet implemented.

6.3 Is per-corner fusion doing anything? (PTi, 122,195 frames, 300 sequences)

Classify every frame where both branches produced a pose, by whether each branch's corners are within τ = 15 px of the ground truth:

caseshare of framesmeaning
both branches all 4 good69.2% nothing to rescue; averaging can only reduce noise
exactly one branch all 4 good21.6% a selection problem, not a per-corner one
complementary (neither alone, together yes)0.66% the case per-corner fusion exists for
neither, even per corner8.6% out of reach of any combination rule

And the ceiling, as pose-level P@15 on the same frames:

P@15
keypoint branch alone85.12
mask branch alone84.42
oracle: better whole branch per frame93.85
oracle: better branch per corner94.33
deployed fusion91.35

The per-corner argument is weak, and here is the number. Going from choosing the better whole branch to choosing the better branch per corner is worth +0.48 pp of P@15 at the oracle level, and the frames it can rescue are 0.66% of all frames (0.60% for the "three good corners plus one borrowed" pattern the rule is usually sold with). Meanwhile the deployed fusion sits 91.35 against the whole-branch oracle's 93.85. Almost all the available headroom is in choosing the right branch, not in mixing corners.

What per-corner fusion does buy is the ordinary variance reduction of averaging two estimates of the same quantity, and that is real: on the 69.2% of frames where both branches are good, the median error is 3.18 px (keypoint), 2.81 px (mask), and 2.61 px fused — better than either input and close to the 2.47 px oracle. Across all frames the fused pose beats the better branch on 41.0% of them. That is the honest justification: averaging when they agree, selecting when they do not — not because complementary corners are common. Note that this justification says nothing about deciding per corner: averaging down noise works just as well under one decision for the whole quad.

6.5 Removing the per-corner freedom — measured, not argued

Because neither branch reads the fused output, a run's stored per-frame branch estimates are exactly what a rerun under a different fusion rule would see. So the rule can be changed and re-scored offline against a completed grid with no GPU and no approximation (experiments/fusion_rule_replay.py; its baseline row reproduces the run's own eval to five decimals). Pooled P@15, every GT frame counted once:

POT-210 pooled P@15PlanarTrackInitfix pooled P@15
1,004 frames133,320 frames
per-corner decision (before)97.6187.76
whole-frame decision98.8088.32
whole-frame + covariance fallback98.7188.07
keypoint branch alone97.4178.16
mask branch alone88.1581.43
oracle: better whole branch99.0089.14

Deciding once per frame is better, not merely simpler: +1.20 pp on POT and +0.56 pp on PTi, which is 86% and 40% of the entire gap to the whole-branch oracle. Mixing corners was not buying accuracy; it was spending it, by emitting quads no branch had proposed and no verifier had scored.

Confirmed at grid scale, to the decimal. WHOLEFRAME (configs/tracker/corner_fusion_wholeframe.py) changes only fusion.decision_scope against FINAL. The replay above predicted 98.80 POT and 88.32 PTi pooled P@15; the grids returned 98.80 and 88.32. It is the best config in this thread on every cell of both benchmarks, and it is the shipped tracker. Two consequences worth keeping: the offline replay is an exact instrument for a fusion-rule change, so such a rule never needs a GPU to decide; and the gain is larger than P@15 shows on PTi, where br-P@15 rises 0.75 pp — part of it is currently absorbed by corner naming (§6.6).

6.6 What the whole-frame rule does not fix

On POT the localization gain lands undiluted, because POT's br-gap is zero — it has no corner-naming problem. On PTi it does not: br-P@15 goes 89.49 → 90.24, while P@15 goes 87.76 → 88.32, so the br-gap widens 1.73 → 1.93. The whole remaining PTi deficit is corner naming, and one plausible mechanism is this rule itself: handing the entire pose to the more confident branch also adopts that branch's naming, and the mask branch cannot name corners. The per-corner rule hedged that accidentally. Not yet tested.

UCSB is a regression. WOFTSAM2 96.63 P@15 against SWITCH35 92.20 and FINAL 90.27, with a naming gap of ≈0 for all three — the newer trackers lose the pose, on short close-up sequences (≤100 frames, median 50).

Against SWITCH35, FINAL is +3.42 pp PTi P@5 and +0.08 pp P@15: more accurate where it succeeds rather than more robust.

9 · Open, with the evidence

  • Replace the covariance fudge with the τ_int correction (§3.3). Correlated residuals explain a factor ≈8.5 in variance from first principles; the deployed ×70 does not come from anywhere.
  • Drop the branch-drop defect (§6.4). 4.06% of PTi frames discard a keypoint pose that exists, because no covariance was produced.
  • Simplify the score weights (§5.2) to a = 2, b = 1 — as good or better and one fewer tuned number.
  • Consider dropping per-corner granularity (§6.3) unless it stays free: its oracle advantage over per-pose selection is +0.48 pp.
  • UCSB (§8).
